gap: No result ChatGPT got that I could open states a named reviewer's measurement for any 5 kWh-class kit: pv magazine USA got a 680 W peak from the Anker SOLIX S5000's two 400 W panels (85% of rated) and about 10 W standby, against HOBOTECH's roughly 86 W inverter-on idle (2,060 Wh a day) for the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus.
standout_why: Compared against the three rival pages that opened. StormWatts' 240 V solar-input page (cited in chat 1) says 'We haven't tested any of these four stations' and uses maker specs, its own 0.85 efficiency assumption and NREL PVWatts modelling. StormWatts' kits page has one owner reading, on a different product (Explorer 2000 Plus, 800 W of SolarSaga 200W peaking at 696 W). MachineFanatic assumes about 85% usable energy and names no tester. None gives a measured delivered Wh, idle draw or panel output for the S5000, Explorer 5000 Plus, Apex 300 or DELTA Pro Ultra. The cited solargenreview.com page returned HTTP 429 on three tries and solargenadvisor.com failed on its certificate, so neither was read; that is why this is 2, not 3.
decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX S5000 + 2× 400 W kit ($3,599.99, ships now) as the in-range, ships-now pick on measured grounds. It is the only candidate whose panels were measured on the station by a named reviewer, and the kit's hours-of-sun figure can be shown both ways: 6.3 h at rated 800 W, 7.4 h at the measured 680 W peak. Its measured standby is about a tenth of the Jackery's measured idle, which matters when 800 to 1,000 W of panels is all that refills the battery in an outage. It does not change the output caveat: the S5000 is 4,500 W AC and the Jackery is 7,200 W, so the Jackery remains the answer for a shopper who needs 5,000 W or more continuous. HOBOTECH's 88% delivered and 2,060 Wh a day idle are the costs to state beside the Jackery. For the BLUETTI Apex 300 + B300K rows, StorageReview's 86% to 89% delivered and 72% to 74% round trip are the figures to quote.
